content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines on the administration and dosage of iron supplements to prevent and control iron-deficiency anemia in infants and children. These guidelines are based on evidence-informed recommendations and aim to assist policymakers, healthcare providers, and program implementers in designing and scaling up effective public health interventions. Iron-deficiency anemia is a significant global health issue, affecting approximately 300 million children worldwide as of 2011. It is most prevalent among children under five years of age and women, with the highest burden observed in South Asia and central and west Africa. Anemia is characterized by a reduction in the number of red blood cells or hemoglobin concentration, impairing the blood's ability to transport oxygen. Iron deficiency, the most common cause of anemia, can result from inadequate dietary intake, poor absorption, increased requirements during growth or pregnancy, blood loss (e.g., menstruation or parasitic infections), or chronic diseases. Iron is an essential nutrient for immune function, neural development, energy metabolism, and physical growth. Approximately 38–62% of anemia cases are responsive to iron supplementation, although this percentage is lower in malaria-endemic regions. Iron-deficiency anemia has been linked to impaired cognitive and motor development in children and reduced productivity in adults. While iron supplementation has shown benefits in improving some developmental outcomes, the effects are inconsistent, and some impairments may be irreversible. The WHO recommends daily oral iron supplementation as a public health intervention for infants and children in settings where anemia prevalence is high (≥40%). Specific recommendations include: 1. Infants and Young Children (6–23 months): Daily supplementation with 2 mg of elemental iron per kilogram of body weight is recommended to prevent iron deficiency and anemia. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 2. Preschool-Age Children (24–59 months): Daily supplementation with 30 mg of elemental iron for three consecutive months each year is recommended to improve hemoglobin levels and iron status. This is a strong recommendation, although the quality of evidence is very low. 3. School-Age Children (5–12 years): Daily supplementation with 30–60 mg of elemental iron for three consecutive months each year is recommended to prevent iron deficiency and anemia. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. Evidence indicates that iron supplementation does not increase the risk of clinical malaria or death when adequate malaria surveillance and treatment services are in place. The WHO emphasizes that daily iron supplementation is a preventive strategy at the population level. In cases where anemia prevalence is between 20–40%, intermittent iron supplementation regimens may be considered. Screening for anemia prior to supplementation is not necessary in settings with high anemia prevalence. The guideline development process involved systematic reviews of evidence, expert consultations, and adherence to the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. The recommendations aim to support countries in achieving global nutrition targets and the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those related to ending hunger and improving nutrition. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of various experts, organizations, and donors, including the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, for their support in developing these guidelines. The recommendations supersede previous WHO guidelines on iron supplementation in children and provide a comprehensive framework for addressing iron-deficiency anemia as a public health priority.
